despite my playtime as of the review, ive enjoyed the game. its great! in my opinion, worth the price. sure, it has its vices, what game doesnt? the game isnt realistic to real life hacking, but i think its hard to make a game thats realistic and fun when it comes to hacking and/or programming games as it will be only for a specific audience which reduces who would play and enjoy the game by alot. its a bit repetitive with how hacking to most systems is the same, but i enjoyed many puzzles that this game provided, especially in the labyrinth DLC. this game isnt perfect, no game is but id say its honestly the closest of any games of this genre that i played. the music is one of the few game soundtracks that i actually liked and would listen to in my spare time. the multiple times that arent just port openers are fun and useful!... well most of them (looking at you, Clock.exe). but id say that some are underused, like the log creator and opener, theyre required to be used i think 2-3 times, but the gap between their uses is too big which makes those tools easily forgettable and can make some puzzles hard to impossible without googling how to solve them. id also say that the map can sometimes be hard to use with time, as if youre looking for a specific server, its hard to find it due to there being so many, even with the map organiser tool provided in the labyrinth DLC. i also love how the trace mechanic isnt an immediate game over like in other hacking games where there are also traces, instead you get a saving grace thats (in my opinion) too easy to complete once youve done it once as the process doesnt change if you need to do it many times. i also love how you can use either the GUI or visual part to play the game or the terminal, you are rarely forced to use either. the many customisation options are very fun and well made, they give you a fresh look at your game, either just changing how it looks to where some things are placed. and then theres the story, now im not an emotional personal and ill admit, i havent cried at the ending but i loved it and felt sorry for our favorite guy, especially after the ending cutscene. i had to replay the game to realise that what he meant is that the remaining copy is ours, the actual game. the labyrinth dlc also messes with the games directory, i would have loved to see more of this mechanic but i more than understand why it isnt used as it would likely get annoying. i also really like how there are what i presume are steam keys, i doubt there are any unredeemed keys after 8 years so i dont know what the keys are for, but its a nice gesture. the dev speaking to us after completing the game and letting us know the ips for some fun servers like "cheaters stash" basically letting us get most binary files (port openers and trace stopper) and others. the labyrinths ending is definitely an unexpected twist and while the choice doesnt matter its still nice to have one. i also immensely enjoyed the labyrinth DLC (if you havent noticed already), i enjoyed how the mission and hub actually looked like and the addition of letting us communicate with the others despite our inability to speak. it could also potentially be used if there was a multiplayer, like a race or trying to speedrun many preset missions, either trying to help or stall your friends and you could communicate as a nice feature, maybe making info on server1 vital to help solve a puzzle on server2 or something like that. also the amount of secrets or easter eggs there are is a very nice and fun addition. the shells are imo underused and their trap is rarely used, i think i used it like once or twice on my second playthrough and it actually did something. and there are the fan made DLCs which is great, you can still play even after you complete the actual game.

In short: i enjoyed the game very much, the characters (which are unfortunately few) are lovable. the game has its vices but those are few and often just mild annoyances. ill definitely be replaying the game and its DLC aswell as the fan made ones. its worth its price, but if you think its not for you, you can wait for a discount.

review_text_raw:
This is gonna be a lengthy review. I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.

When I first went to view the page for this game, there were many questions that began flooding my mind. And now that I've played the game almost to its entirety, I think that I can answer most of these questions that interested consumers passing by may have. This game was a real treat, and I think that it deserves more attention than it's received.


[h1] Is Hacknet realistic? [/h1]

If you mean "realistic" as in "Is this game close to hacking in real life?" then the answer is no. This game is not realistic because it is fun and doesn't make you paranoid. You are in possession of a bunch of hacking tools that put up the kinds of graphics you'd expect to be running on computers in a 90's hacker film, and the way these tools work is by executing them and waiting for the flashy hacking graphics to stop flashing so that you can run another flashy hacker tool until you gain administrative system access. Granted, it's more complex than that, which is why this game is really enjoyable, but you're not going to be writing complex algorithms to overload proxy servers and bypass tracing measures. That's what the 90's tools are for.

That being said, this may be as close as gaming will ever come to realistic hacking. Because anything that tries to be precicely like real hacking that doesn't give you fancy hacker programs probably isn't going to be a very fun game. And this, again, is a fun game. The entire game takes place on a computer's operating system, and every hack you perform is done through this system. In addition, the commands you use are based on real UNIX commands, even if the commands are typically used to activate the previously-mentioned hacking programs. It's certainly more realistic than games where you push a button and your character goes [i]"I'm in" [/i] like Watch_Dogs and Quadrilateral Cowboy (That isn't to say that they're bad games, just that they're not trying to be realistic hacking simulations which, again, isn't necessarily a bad thing).


[h1] Is this game immersive? Will I feel like a hacker even if I'm not performing real hacks? [/h1]

Oh, yes. If you want to feel like the genius hacker that always appears in Hollywood films but rarely gets any time for actual character development, then this game is for you. The presentation of this game is great, and it really helps to sell that feeling of accomplishment that you get when you pull off a successful job. After about 30 minutes in, I had to re-check the steam store to make sure that I wasn't accessing a multiplayer hacking simulator. But nope, I was even able to play this game in airplane mode. As the store page mentions, there are very few things that break the immersion by being obvious parts of a video game. To complete a job, you email the client explaining that you've finished. To acquire a new tool, you have to copy said tool to your home computer from its rightful owner. 

And this immersive presentation goes a long way in the overall experience. I know that not everybody responds the same way, but I found certain parts to incite genuine emotion in a way that few other games have managed to pull off. Like when you're given the option to accept a job in which [spoiler]you have to euthanize a dying man by hacking his pacemaker [/spoiler], or when [spoiler]you run "OpenCDtray" on your own system and your real computer's disc tray opens and may potentially scare the hell out of you[/spoiler]. So even if you're using overpowered tools to open systems that nobody bothers to check, you'll probably still feel really good doing so.


[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1]

No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out.


[h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1]

Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review.


[h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1]

I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times.


[h1] TL;DR [/h1]

This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you. The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect. NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

1. You can't finish all contracts. At some point the game will just tell you "You're good enough for more difficult tasks" and a main quest will trigger, blocking you from accepting new quests. You can never go back and you can't do them after the final mission.

2. You can't create files or directories. Organizing your downloaded files is annoying because you can only use the pre-defined ones. In one contract you're supposed to forge a file, and that works by downloading a file and editing the copy...

3. You can't remove directories. There's almost never a need to do so, but when you need to remove the contents from a directory with multiple subdirectories, you need to access each subdir individually and remove the contents.

4. Autocomplete doesn't add a whitespace after the autocompleteted word. Confusing as hell for a regular terminal user.

5. The final mission consists of multiple phases, which each one explaining your next goal. In phase 3 you're supposed to send a password but you aren't told so. I just used the password I found to login and continued my quest. After a while I got stuck, and after more than an hour I finally looked into a walkthrough - and learnt that I needed to send the password instead of entering it, and that had already solved the final mission by myself over an hour ago. At least I could just click the "complete quest" button 4 times in a row to trigger the ending.

6. The gameplay is quite repetetive. Connect to a server, open the closed ports (which always works the same, for all of them), find the file you need. There are only 2 missions that go beyond that and actually force you to think: The final mission, and the mission before. That doesn't really speak for the game.

7. The map is just plain awful. It's cluttered with nodes from earlier contracts which you never need to connect to anymore. Literally hardest part of the game is finding the correct node on the map.

8. Secrets. Don't get me wrong, secrets are great. But I looked into a guide after finishing the game, and some secrets didn't trigger for me although I definitely satisfied their conditions. So maybe I shouldn't have written "Secrets", but "Bugs". Furthermore, some secrets get you hyped, and when you finally solve their puzzle, you get... a digital clock that even uses up your RAM?

9. Alt+Tab closes the game.

I completed the game in a single session. It was kinda fun, although way too easy. But damn, some of the issues I just mentioned are pissing me off and I'm not going to play the DLC or any user-created mod.

At a time when the average movie-goer is getting increasingly skeptical of 'hacking scenes' that showcase multi-dimensional Rubik's cubes interlinked in cyberspace, Hacknet does a pretty good job of capturing that disillusionment with a game that's closer to reality.

This game could be used to simulate hacking in movies, especially since you can create custom extensions/mods with their own back stories.

Pro's

+ Not much of a fancy GUI or Hollywood-style effects. It's possible to disable the GUI and go terminal-only.
+ Real unix commands to interact with the file system.

Con's

- Might feel lacklustre if you have used Linux before and/or already know some security jargon.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. review_text_raw:
This is an OK game. I wouldn't go as far as to compare it to either Uplink or the Street Hacker series simply because it feels more like a demo when compared to them. The execution and gameplay is shallow and naive. It's plagued by many basic design issues and most of the missions are just boring, repetitive, and feel more like a chore rather than a challenge.

My biggest gripes are:
-boring, repetitive and easy missions. Only 2 interesting missions stand out, the final Bit one, and the online pacemaker one.
-no sense of urgency or challenge. If you get caught hacking, that's just a reload to last checkpoint. No point in deleting any logs the way Uplink makes sure that you do. Uplink kept you on your toes because getting caught meant absolute game over!
-Badly designed UI. The workstation "map" is a cluttered mess especially as you move closer towards the end. Nodes are being randomly generated and the ones closest to the edge of the screen have their hover information cut off. How that ever went past the testers, I do not know!
-Weird writing, bad grammar, spelling mistakes, juvenile jokes scattered here and there. The ending was incredibly cheesy and anti-climactic.

Not a bad game to get on sale. But this is no Uplink for sure. The tagline shouldn't be "if you liked Uplink, you'll love this!" It's more the other way around because now I definitely feel like going back and replaying Uplink for the zillionth time! :)

After completing Hacknet and it's Labirynths expansion I believe that the game is worth experiencing for the price it asks.

The Good:
- 8h campaign (I did some NOT ALL side missions and the Labirynth expansion)
- Interesting storylines
- Moral Disconnect/Dilemmas
- Simplicity                                   < Easy to understand, just a bit hard to remember commands etc.
- Workshop Support                     < People made some very awesome mods.
- Visuals                                        < It makes your screen look suspicious

The Bad:
- Simplicity
- Slightly difficult to navigate "network map" < Yes I am aware of the existence of the sorter. I still think it could be better in some way.

My wishlist:
- More complexity in the puzzles.
- Clearer more understandable map.
- More ways to solve objectives.
- Hardware Customisation.

Conclusion:
A very pleasant experience with possible extension via the mods on the workshop. Decent story with some interesting twists. The hacking gameplay becomes quite repetitive with time, as it just requires you to think what tool to use for each port. The investigative gameplay is actually surprisingly fun, the game leaves you with enough hints to go on, however the game rarely offers a situation to decide the outcome or change the approach to completing objective. In a certain sense it is linear.

review_text_raw:
I'll say it straight, I am not a hacker or an expert programmer, although I had a minimal use of console clients and some programming basics, beside using consoles like DOS in my very first PCs. Hacknet is a hacking game entirely done through console commands and minimal interface in a fictional OS, you'll join tasks to do to go through a main story and a few side jobs, most of the game is all about typing codes on console, the faster you go the better you hack, there are just a few times you must stop and think how to proceed to get the informations or files you need, which is nothing impossible for a beginner. I liked this game for it's way to be different, not too difficult to learn, not too far from reality. 


[b][u]PROS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]HACKING[/u]: There's not much space for hacking effects, beside a few simple animations, hacking goes all through a console, and that's the way real hackers work! The way it makes you feel is great, with some basic commands you can do anything you want without being an IT expert, actually teaching one thing or two about real hacking and consoles! I enjoyed this version of hacking better than unrealistic interactive ways from other games, thumbs up!

[*][u]DIFFICULTY[/u]: Difficulty is very balanced, at least for someone with my experience, it's all about learning a dozen commands, understand what they do and use them for your purposes, not too hard, neither too easy. Once you understand how to use them, you need to get faster and use logic to find what you need, which could be a hidden file or password, beginners shouldn't have too many problems, intermediates woul enjoy it, experts maybe would find it a bit too easy and boring.

[*][u]MINIMAL[/u]: Its minimal graphics just plays a good role, real hackers don't use animations and such, leaving it minimal gives it some realism and fashion, plus makes the game lighter. Thanks for leaving it as minimal as it would be in real hacking, with just very few add ons.

[*][u]STORY AND BACKSTORY[/u]: At first I had the feeling it was short and easy...and I was right, although the climax near the end was awesome, got me stuck into knowing the ending of it and hack into the very last hard tasks, I had to change my opinion about the story, it was good and interesting! There's a bit of backstory about the making of the game, explained by the developer himself, which makes the game's finale even better.

[*][u]WORKSHOP[/u]: I noticed the workshop is enabled and has extra missions and stories to download and play. I admit I didn't try anything from the workshop yet, but sounds like you can expand your game with some addons, which compensaty the main story's shortness and the game's price.

[*][u]SMOOTH AND LIGHT[/u]: Being mostly on console and so minimal, the game runs great on PC with very low hardware requirement. As far as the gameplay experience and fun are untouched, it's a good strong point to distribute the game to low end and PCs not made for gaming.


[/list]


[b][u]CONS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]EYE BOILING[/u]: I've spent about 23 years in front of screens, starting from old CRTs, despite that I never had problems with my sight, either glasses or hurting eyes for long times. Despite that, Hacknet was the first and only game to give me eye pain, not fully sure if my sight is just failing or had a tiring day, but it never happened before. Watching the console for a few hours was a lot worse than I ever experienced before. So be careful, you may need some eye resting from time to time or just not play it for too long.

[*][u]END MISSION EMAILS[/u]: Just like real tasks, you don't win as soon as you reach your objective, most of times you need to send an email back to the contact and it will say if you completed your mission or not. Some tasks requires to write a password in the reply, that way you know what you need to find and what you need to write, but most of times it's all about sending a blank email back, if you didn't complete it, you'll get an error while trying to send the email. To cut it short, there are times you just need to access to files or servers and then answer the email, sometimes your objective is not so clear, so you will get stuck in the email before you fry your mind thinking about stuff you may have skipped or fry the game by reading a step-by-step guide, which kills the fun from the game. There were a few times that frustrated me, maybe giving more informations about the task or send back an email to give hints about the missing tasks would have been better.

[*][u]STORY LENGTH[/u]: Even if short and simple, I praised the story for its climax, but I can't hide a bit of disappointment for being so short, about 9-12 hours for the story, 3-4 extra hours to complete achievements and the other contracts and about 3-4 hours for the DLC (which I don't own nor tried). would have been perfect to almost double its time to make the game truly worth its price, but at least the workshop should help a bit more.

[/list]

Final word: Not too easy, not too hard, made for newbies curious about hacking and people with a bit of knowledge about it. If you accept the compromise to "play" on the console only, it will give you a true hacking feeling and about 10 hours of fun, and I loved it. Recommended for those people, especially if you can find it for a good price!

This is one of those games that makes you wish for a 'meh' rating. I'm three hours in and the narrative isn't really picking up. The soundtrack is excellent, the use of real console commands is cool, and hacking feels pretty fun -- it scratches that fantasy of being a shady, smart hacker... but provides none of the challenge. The hacking is easy and the contracts largely repetitive outside of a few good gags. There's no real moral choices and ultimately, the game just doesn't hook you in as much after a while. A stronger narrative, more choices and better puzzles would serve this game well. The best moment I experienced came when I was counter-hacked, and had to reboot my system by navigating only with the terminal. But the moment-to-moment gameplay requires no such thought.

Still, a lot of people seem to enjoy that core fantasy and find the narrative engaging enough to keep going, and if you're really into the game, the mod support is excellent. 

Tl;dr it's fine, if you enjoy the core fantasy a lot there's a lot of good stuff there for you, but otherwise it's let down by disappointing gameplay.

review_text_raw:
Lemme start by saying that this feels like it'd be a pretty niche title.  If the idea of entering commands into a terminal and making notes about IP addresses and passwords does not appeal to you, then turn away now since that's the majority of the gameplay here.


Hacknet fits into the very, very tiny genre of hacking games.  No, not Watch Dogs.  More like Uplink.  And... umm... others?  I honestly don't know of any other titles in this genre, to be honest!  It's a game about breaking into servers, looking for information, and then covering your tracks.  As the game progresses, you'll be tested on your ability to type accurately, multi-task quickly, and ability to dig deep for details in order to progress.  It's a satisfying experience, but I can see where this can get incredibly frustrating, or boring, for some.

Note:  I do not own the DLC and, therefore, it does not factor into this review.

The Good

-Somewhat simulates Real Life™ hacking, versus the "Hollywood" hacking used in Uplink.  It's cool, but I imagine its very simplied and toned down.  But, it's still really neat.

-Makes a fairly daunting premise pretty easy to figure out and play.  The tutorials explain things well enough and stuff isn't thrown at you too fast.  You won't get turned loose on your own until you have a firm grasp of things and you'll never get in over your head.

-Meanwhile, the game is still challenging enough you'll have to stop and think things through at times or get put into situations where the pressure is on and you can't afford to make mistakes.  

-Good music.  It's not great music, persay, but it sets the mood well and isn't distracting.  Not something I'd plan on listening to out of the game, but I definitely appreciate its presence.

-Workshop support is always a good thing to have in a game.  I've not tried the stuff out yet, but it seems like people can do things like add new missions and stuff, which is cool and can add a lot of longevity to the game.


The Neutral

-The plot...  its serviceable, but a bit predictable.  Kinda a shrug rating.


The Bad

-The cost might be one of them.  The game isn't very long and, combined with the next point, might make $10 a little steep.  Granted, there's incredibly few games in this sort of genre and mod support will help shore up the major short coming.

-The big, big, big point though, is the game is short and fairly linear and, therefore, has low replay value.  There's secrets to explore and discover and some parts of the game are procedurally generated, making for a somewhat different experience each time.  However, it lacks the open nature of Uplink, its progression systems, or two options of storylines.  Tools are given when you needed them, no sooner and no later.  Side unlock stuff are mostly cosmetic things, like new themes.  There's very few side missions and you'll have to do most of them to progress either way.  You're looking at 5-6 hours for a single play through and it'll feel like it's over just a little bit too soon.  This is no doubt the biggest thing to consider when thinking about buying this game.  Although, remember, Workshop support can potentially alleviate this issue.

-The server map gets rather unwieldly late game, as its hard to tell which server is which or select the right one.  Some sort of filtering tool would have been a huge help here, especially since most servers only get used once or twice and then never again.


All in all, this is a tough recommendation.  It's a fairly niche title and you may wish to wait for a sale to pick it up.  But there's very, very few experiences on the market that are anything like it, so it's definitely worth giving a shot if only for novelty's sake.

review_text_raw:
Overview:
  Hacknet is at its heart a digital exploration game. Using a powerful suite of programs that you gain throughout the game, the player must gain access to systems and perform contracts. The game has a very similar feeling to the older game Uplink and hacking is done through speed, knowledge of your tools, and system resource management (RAM).

Plot:
  The plot is pretty threadbare, but does a good job of pulling the overarching story together. The ending makes sense, but is a little lacklustre for the scope of what you supposedly accomplish. However, this is in character for hacking since public attention is bad for those at the fringe of legality. Overall, I enjoyed the plot, but the beginning intro and ending are really the only interesting points. It's difficult to do characterization when all you have is text, but I felt that more effort could have been put into letting the player get to know more of the other people in the story (naix, maybe some backstory on bit, etc.)
 
Gameplay:
  The gameplay is separated into two parts: hacking and forensics. The actual hacking is rather easy since most trace timers last far more than long enough and some systems actually keep your admin after you disconnect. The main challenge in this format is simply knowing which order to run the port hacking programs in so that you can maximize efficiency and minimize time spent not logged in. These do get quite intense at times and a few conflict sequences definitely run the point home that you're not invulnerable. Progress through the game is blocked in a sort of metroid-vania way, in the sense that you need this power to unlock that type of port to enter. I enjoyed this, but wished that there were more early systems that you needed to backtrack to.

  That backtracking is part of the second part of the gameplay, the forensics. By this I mean that you spend your time going through file systems trying to spot the file with the password, scanning computers to reach connected nodes, and searching for new IPs to check out. In fact, there is an entirely alternative gameplay path that is only reached with diligent use of your tools. I loved the exploring, but it did feel quite limited, or at the very least truncated to be more accessable for players who might not be used to the gameplay style.
  Part of the joy of the exploration comes from the humor that you find in random files. From a script for "Titanic 2" that involves the icebergs running onto land and attacking people to Bash.org IRC logs, there is a decent amount of silliness and joy to discover. However, since the files in the systems you hack are procedurally generated, more content would have been nice. There's only so many times that you can see the same Bash log before you stop wanting 
to check them out because you feel you've seen everything.

Pros:
*really fun
*sense of satisfaction from difficult hacks
*humor: From a mission where you need to write "d*cks" on the main webpage of "Nortron Security" to an homage to *chans (the secret /el/ image board), the game is very funny and self aware.
*exploration
*failure penalty fair
*short: Hacknet doesn't wear out its welcome, which it probably would have for some players by the end game.

Cons:
*repetitive
*short
*not enough content
*exploration feels like it was stunted for ease of access

Hopes:
*mods:
	I feel that mods could make this from a good game to a great game. I'd love to try my hand at adding new features to the game.
*hardware changes
	Uplink let the player purchase hardware upgrades to increase ram or processing power as well as giving access to more complicated systems. Hacknet's only customization for your computer is changing the display theme.
*more story
	Getting to know the other hackers more personally would be very enjoyable.
*higher difficulty
	clearing the logs on a system means that they won't track you down - but this presents a problem. You always leave a disconnect log, but the game doesn't notice that a disconnect log without a matching connect log implies
	that the IP that disconnected was responsible for the attack. Having to selectively clear logs and/or bounce IP like Uplink might be a good idea. In addition, I would have enjoyed more difficult forensics and encrypted files
	that you can't find the password for. I was a little miffed a few times when I spent some time looking through the files to find the next IP when all I had to do was type "scan". More threats to the player as well as uncertainty
	in how well you performed the attack would be welcome.
*more challenges
	Maybe adding in new network architecture requiring the player to do a different minigame than typing the first two letters of a program and tab completing.
*multiplayer
	multiplayer is hinted at being in development in the files on the endgame server.

Bottom Line:
I love this game and want to spend so much more time on it, but sadly it seems that there's no more content. This type of game is sadly lacking in today's market and is quite unique. It pulls off what it does well and with much better guidance than Uplink. You should try it if you're interested in learning basic cmd/*nix commands and command line navigation/use while having fun, if you like tech and silly games, or if you're a fan of Uplink.

review_text_raw:
This is a great hacking game that uses command prompts in order to do things. The game begins with you receiving an email via a Dead Man Switch, which is something that is sent if certain conditions are met(or not), such as not turning on your computer for a week. This email sent to you was from a Hacker named Bit. He didn't log on after 2 weeks, so the email was auto sent to you. It said that 'if you're reading this, I'm already dead'. The game continues into a tutorial where you complete the tasks that Bit set up to be sent to you as you finish them.

This is the premise of the story(no spoilers in that btw). You go through this hacking world trying to find out what happened to bit. You can explore the various computers you come across in your travels, read the various text documents that can contain story related content, whether it be main quest or side quest, or joke texts. There's a site called Bash.org in real life, and it archives funny quotes that people submit that the found on various IRC(chat rooms) conversations. Hacknet is filled with many text documents, usually starting with "IRC" then numbers. They're very funny, and you can even collect them if you wish.

Hacknet is a lot like Uplink, but more modern and polished. There's organizations that give you missions/side quests for you to do, and they're all interesting in some way. The side quests are required to a fair degree, as Bits messages wont tell you more until your skill improves by going up in rank on these Organizations. It's not just randomly generated quests like in Uplink, where the differences in quests was basically names and numbers. All of Hacknets Side Quests/Missions have little stories, and as you do these contracts, you may end up finding text documents that hint at what happened to Bit.

For the actual gameplay, it starts out simple, with a few programs to help break through security You'll find more programs to help you get into more complicated systems. 

Now for how Hacknet is different from Uplink. For one thing, there's no upgrades. You can find hacking programs, but there's no upgrading, no hacking store to buy hacking upgrades/software. There's no money actually, and no upgrading your computer. Instead of grinding money to get a more powerful PC and just bulldoze your way through security in Uplink, you need to use your programs and computer more strategically.

This DOSE lower replay value compared to Uplink. In Uplink there's plenty of things to buy and upgrade, and unlimited, if not plain, missions to do. Hacknet is more story driven, with it's main story and the little side stories filled with interesting jobs, info, chat logs, and lots of other things.

I'm not sure how far I am exactly, but at the very least, there's about 35+ side quests at the very least. So there's plenty to do in this game, along with Easter eggs and subtle references to entertain you.

While Uplink was more mouse driven in how you hack, Hacknet is almost entirely with keyboard commands, like Spencer's Hacker Evolution games(The first 2, not the shitty Duality). There is some mouse controls, such as using the mouse to quickly move through a computers directories.

If you like Uplink, you will definitely like Hacknet. If you're interested in hacking games, but haven't played one before, this COULD be a good start, as the difficulty curve is very fair, but Uplink might be better for a newbie.

Btw, you can use the TAB key to auto complete words/directories/programs names. Useful for when you need to quickly break through many ports.

Developed by Team Fractal Alligator, the game places players in the role of a recently deceased hacker whose death was mysteriously logged in the system, prompting you to follow their digital footsteps through a series of hacking tasks. From the moment you begin, Hacknet pulls you into a gritty, text-based cyber world that relies heavily on realistic command-line interfaces, compelling storytelling, and a sense of discovery that is rarely found in traditional puzzle or adventure games.

At its core, Hacknet is all about learning and using real-world hacking concepts in a fictional setting. The gameplay revolves around typing actual Unix-based commands, running scripts, cracking passwords, and exploiting network vulnerabilities. Unlike many games that simplify hacking into a series of quick minigames or button presses, Hacknet demands attention to detail and encourages experimentation. The command line interface is intuitive yet detailed, and the game introduces commands gradually, allowing players to build a solid understanding of the mechanics as they progress. The pacing strikes a perfect balance between tutorialization and challenge, making it approachable for newcomers without feeling watered down for those with some technical knowledge.

The narrative is one of the standout features of Hacknet. It unfolds through in-game emails, chat logs, and system messages, painting a picture of a shadowy digital underworld filled with intrigue, moral ambiguity, and complex characters. You’re not just hacking for the sake of hacking; there is an overarching mystery and a compelling story that motivates your actions. The writing is sharp, immersive, and at times surprisingly emotional, which elevates the experience beyond a purely mechanical simulation. The game’s episodic structure ensures that the story unfolds organically, revealing new layers and twists as you delve deeper into the cyber realm.

Visually, Hacknet embraces a minimalist aesthetic that perfectly suits its subject matter. The black terminal screen with green and white text, simple window layouts, and sparse but effective use of icons and alerts all contribute to a tense, focused atmosphere. This stark visual style keeps distractions at bay and mirrors the real-world hacking environment, which is often devoid of flashy graphics or unnecessary clutter. Sound design is subtle but impactful—the ambient electronic soundtrack and occasional notification sounds create a sense of urgency and immersion without overwhelming the player.

One of the game’s greatest strengths lies in its open-ended approach to problem-solving. While certain missions have specific goals, there are often multiple ways to achieve them, encouraging players to think creatively and strategically. Tools can be upgraded and customized, and players must learn to manage limited resources like access time and software capabilities. This encourages careful planning and prioritization, and often rewards lateral thinking and patience. The inclusion of realistic constraints, such as the risk of being traced or locked out, adds tension and stakes to each hacking attempt.

The community surrounding Hacknet has also contributed significantly to its longevity. The game supports modding, and players have created custom missions, alternate storylines, and new tools that expand the gameplay experience far beyond the base game. This openness to user-generated content keeps the game fresh and provides a platform for those interested in exploring hacking concepts in even more depth.

While Hacknet is highly praised, it’s important to note that its appeal is somewhat niche. Players looking for fast-paced action or high-octane thrills might find the methodical, text-heavy gameplay slow or dense. The learning curve, though well-managed, can be steep for those unfamiliar with command-line interfaces or hacking terminology. However, for players fascinated by computers, cybersecurity, or puzzle-solving, Hacknet offers a deeply satisfying and often enlightening experience that feels genuinely rewarding.

In conclusion, Hacknet stands out as a rare title that successfully combines educational value with compelling storytelling and engaging gameplay mechanics. Its realistic portrayal of hacking, grounded in authentic command-line use, sets it apart from other cyber-themed games that often rely on gimmicks or unrealistic portrayals. The game’s narrative depth, minimalist yet effective presentation, and open-ended problem-solving create an experience that is both intellectually stimulating and highly entertaining. For anyone curious about the world of hacking or simply looking for a unique puzzle-adventure game, Hacknet is a must-play that continues to impress years after its release.

review_text_raw:
This game is pretty dope.

Gameplay-wise, the actual inputs you'll perform are mainly terminal based. Most of the time you'll be typing commands as rapidly as you can. Actual inputs can be tricky if you need to operate quickly, but the majority of what you'll be doing is essentially puzzle solving. A typical mission in the game requires you to gain access to a given entry point which will contain links or clues that you can follow to the next point, which may contain further clues, etc. That's an incredibly basic description of the game: Actual missions are immersive enough and the actual hints/puzzles/solutions are varied enough that the game is able to stay fresh well through the main campaign and DLC.

The story is pretty cool. (Won't go into spoilers here, what I tell you is what you learn literally within minutes of starting the game.) A notorious hacker who goes by Bit has passed away, and has left you his custom-made hacking software in his wake, along with the request to use it to figure out what killed him and why. You quickly integrate with a local hacker group and start climbing the ranks to gain influence and leads. Along the way you'll acquire (either from your hacker group or by stealing it from a target computer) new tools or methods that allow you to break into more secure devices. Since the game is all text based, you'll only get to know characters via what they've written to you, and it can be tricky to build strong characters that way if the player is impatient. I feel that sticking through and reading the text will greatly benefit your enjoyment of the story of the game as well as of the game overall.

The aesthetic of the game is a big part of it. The entire game is played as though it's not a game. It's as if you have a virtual machine running another OS on your computer. The perspective is never pulled into real life, and you'll never see your character because as far as the game is concerned, YOU in real life are your character. This is an excellent way to build immersion, and you'll find yourself quickly sucked in to the game. The visuals are simplistic but robust and well designed (and even customizable, eventually), and the soundtrack will keep you cool while trying to break into complex systems and get you pumped when it's time to move fast. Just playing the game and becoming immersed is a bit of an experience that can be hard to find elsewhere.

As an aside, I would reccomend the DLC if you enjoy the main game. It tells a story that's basically completely separate from the main game: Essentially it may as well be a sequel. It introduces new systems that compliment the puzzle elements like I mentioned above. The game also features workshop support which contains even more community made campaigns (some as long as the DLC), but many of them require content from the DLC to function.

Tl;dr: Fun game, you'll get immersed if you let yourself and it's a serious blast. Gameplay is essentially puzzle based but at times requires you to be fast too.

Hacknet : By Triple F

In the ever-evolving realm of video games, there are titles that make players question the boundaries of the medium. "Hacknet," developed by Team Fractal Alligator and released in 2015, is one such game. It propels players into the thrilling, complex world of hacking and cyber espionage, offering a unique and immersive experience that challenges the mind, tickles the senses, and leaves an indelible mark on the player. This in-depth review will dive deep into the intricacies of "Hacknet," examining its gameplay, narrative, aesthetics, and overall impact on the gaming landscape.

"Hacknet" plunges players into a visually minimalist but functionally intricate interface reminiscent of the movie "Hackers" and the TV series "Mr. Robot." As a talented hacker, your task is to unravel the mysteries of the recently deceased hacker, Bit, by delving into a network of interconnected nodes. The gameplay is refreshing, as it avoids the traditional button-mashing mechanics prevalent in many other genres. Instead, it relies heavily on typing commands, creating an authentic hacking experience that is both engaging and educational.

The learning curve is steep, and "Hacknet" offers no hand-holding. However, this is one of the game's strengths, encouraging players to master real-world command-line interfaces and computer network protocols. As you progress, you'll become more proficient in executing intricate scripts, deciphering logs, and infiltrating secure servers. The game's missions are intelligently designed, gradually escalating in complexity while maintaining a cohesive narrative thread. The sense of accomplishment that accompanies successfully completing a difficult hack is immensely satisfying.

The only minor drawback is the occasional repetitiveness in mission objectives, but the game counters this with the introduction of various tools and concepts as you advance. The addition of mod support further extends the game-play's lifespan, offering a wealth of user-generated content and challenges.

The narrative framework of "Hacknet" is a cyber-mystery masterpiece. Players are drawn into an enigmatic world where each email, log entry, and terminal command provides a piece of the puzzle. The story is immersive and genuinely suspenseful, keeping players engaged and eager to uncover the truth behind Bit's death and the larger conspiracy at play.

The game's writing is sharp, but it can be slightly overwhelming at times for those unfamiliar with hacker jargon. Nonetheless, it rewards players who pay close attention and invest in the unfolding story. As the narrative unfolds, it explores themes of ethics, morality, and the consequences of one's actions in a digital world, making it a cerebral experience that lingers long after the final keystrokes.

"Hacknet" adopts a minimalist visual style, with predominantly monochromatic screens and simple text-based interfaces. While the graphics may not be visually stunning in the traditional sense, they are perfectly suited to the game's subject matter. The retro-futuristic aesthetics pay homage to classic hacker culture, successfully creating an atmosphere reminiscent of '90s cyberpunk movies.

The game's soundtrack, composed by Evan Gipson, deserves special mention. It expertly complements the gameplay and narrative, immersing players in an electronic symphony of tension and excitement. The sound design further enhances the overall experience, making every keystroke feel significant.

"Hacknet" has had a substantial impact on the gaming landscape. It introduced a unique gameplay experience that blends education with entertainment, inspiring players to delve into the world of coding and hacking. It also sparked a resurgence of interest in hacking-themed games, paving the way for titles like "Quadrilateral Cowboy" and "Mainlining."

Moreover, "Hacknet" has cultivated a dedicated modding community, extending the game's longevity and fostering creativity among its player base. Its open-ended nature encourages experimentation and exploration, making it a digital playground for aspiring hackers and programmers.

In conclusion, "Hacknet" is a digital masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of traditional gaming. It offers an authentic hacking experience, a gripping narrative, and an atmosphere that immerses players in the world of cyber espionage. While its minimalistic aesthetics may not be for everyone, they serve a purpose and enhance the game's overall appeal. With its lasting impact on the gaming industry and the skills it imparts to players, "Hacknet" is more than just a game; it's an educational journey through the digital labyrinth that will continue to inspire and challenge gamers for years to come.

Shall..we..play..a..game?

Welcome to Hacknet, a game that made me feel so much that i was somewhere inside a 80's hacker movie it had me waiting for Joshua to call me to tell me we needed to finish the game we started.

I was really surprised at how much i enjoyed the game being that it is mostly text based but to the details.

The game is niche but even if you have only the most basic and i mean BASIC keyboarding skills you can quickly get the commands down. If you've ever set up your own linux box and just messed around with it a little bit you can play this game. If you watched Wargames, Hackers, Ghost in the Shell, or played Cyberpunk, Shadowrun, or Anarchy Online you will want to play this game. I picked it up during a 75% off sale and only now started playing and it is very addicting and hilarious at the same time. There are some parts that really screw with your mind and so as not to spoil the story let me just say that you must "role play" the persona in the game. When the things that screw with your mind happen you have to ask yourself "What would my "Hacker" persona do?"

The soundtrack is very techno-club and adds to the overall feel of the game nicely.
The learning curve is a bit like a roller coaster and if you aren't paying attention you can find yourself stuck and wondering what to do.

You won't learn to code, or "hack", or script anything. You will get really good practice at some few basic Linux commands in the terminal which is good practice and fun. I haven't found a binary compiler in the game so haven't been able to figure out what the binary code files are or if i'm even supposed to figure out what they are. but it's still fun to wonder.

This game has great multi-player potential but other reviews indicate that the developers may not do any more with it. Also there is no multi-monitor support which would be a really nice touch but isn't likely to happen either.

I've put almost 5 hours at this point; found a bunch of stuff; lost a bunch of stuff; got my stuff back and loved every minute of it. The game won't teach you to be a hacker, but it is the Hacking game you didn't know that you desperately needed to play.

It is a niche game to be sure but if you are feeling a bit nostalgic after the gaming references i've made, download the game and enjoy. I did buy it on very cheap sale, 75% off,  but $10 isn't an excessive price point for a really fun game. I don't see a whole lot of replaying the game due to the linear storyline. Steam community has added some content and there seems to be enough material from the community to make the game worthwhile.

Full disclosure: I am a giant nerd. Grew up more on computers (and dogs!) than, like, ya know.... PEOPLE... The point is, if you put a terminal or a shell in front of me I get super excited and it's instantly, like, +5,000 to appreciation for thing.

ANYWAY.

This game is sublime. I think, oftentimes, if you look up hacking sims, you get to get stuff like Uplink, which is very good, certainly, and I DO recommend it, but Hacknet was made as a spiritual successor to it (by the dev's own confirmation), and I consider it better in every way. Uplink is a little more sandbox-y (think, like, a game that is entirely a radiant quest from Skyrim. Except, like... good. And dynamic); Hacknet actually has a story. There are a number of missions to do, and it's not linear in the sense that you have to do everything in order, but there are a couple factions you can go with and you'll get different tasks from them. It all culminates in the same storyline at the end, but I don't mean that as a negative. Essentially, you encounter external systems and learn to crack them. For various reasons. Everything from "delete this sensitive file" to "modify a file's contents" to "find out where this signal came from" to "cripple this server" and others. And that's just for starters. Eventually you start dealing with conspiracies, and your missions get really involved, having to crack multiple terminals, finding links between them, worming your way into other systems, finding user credentials, reading e-mails, finding synched external devices, etc, etc. You have to break through security before you can CRACK the system, naturally, and different systems have different layers requiring different programs to surpass. It's almost entirely SKiddying, for those of you who are also dorks like myself, but it's very entertainingly-done and the graphics built to illustrate Computer Happenings (R)(C) are really rad. I wouldn't be surprised if you needed a guide at some point, your first time through, but, well, put it this way: collaboration between agents is pretty common, so don't feel bad.

The interface is really cool, you CAN do just about everything with the mouse, if you're wired that way, but you can also use the console, which is my preferred way of doing things. There are multiple .sys overlays you can enable, as well, to change your GUI and layout, which adds a little customization (some of them done by commissioned artist). The expansion that's since come out is a lot of fun, and adds probably another four to six hours to a game that I'd say is around ten hours your first time through, if you know what you're doing. Decently replayable, too.

Finally, I will say that this is one of my favorite soundtracks I've ever heard. I've never seen a game before this that uses Vaporwave as its backing, but it makes a lot of sense; that's a really good genre for focus-demanding work, like this game presents. Also, they used HOME on the soundtrack, and they are one of my absolute favorites (shill, shill). I will also say, while the OST is extremely chill, they DO use one of the higher-octane tracks from Hotline Miami 2, and I daresay it fits even better here.

All in all, you can get the game, its expansion, and both OSTs for twenty bucks, when it ISN'T on sale, and I find that to be a friggin' steal. On a closing note, there's no other game that will actually get your adrenaline pumping entering text commands at a shell. I defy anyone who says they can do the endgame of the original or Labyrinths without a significant spike in vitals.

Pros :

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is not "an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator for PC", this here is just a lie and I actually would say may be a detriment to the game depending on who you are and how you take those words.

If you're like me and you essentially expected a hacking simulator where you did as you please, hacked who you wanted to hack, and cause mayhem or the like, this is not what this game is about. You're better off looking at Uplink and getting UplinkOS.

What you're really getting from Hacknet is actually a sort of immersive novel, but you're a silent protagonist who probably button mashes the keyboard when sending e-mails.

Hacknet is very much the story about a recently deceased hacker named Bit. It's very much about trying to uncover what it was that Bit was doing that got him killed.

Hacknet is not a game you are going to be spending nearly 20 hours of your life playing though. At the moment of writing, I have 17, but that mostly comes from me picking the game back up again in previous attempts to play the game, and realizing that I have no idea what I'm doing at all, and starting back from the beginning to figure out what things did what.

The reality is, this game is actually about 8 hours or so in length, maybe a couple more if you get a tad lost. It's sort of hard to say, I would also wager it could be 10.

[b]But a thumbs up though, why?[/b] Well that's simply because this game does something interesting in all of this, and that is create interesting setups here and there for you to complete. Be it in one instance hacking into a fictional fast food chicken restaurants servers to find their secret recipe, death row records, [i]hospital equipment[/i], or deleting the save file of a user from a clicker game, Hacknet tries to give you interesting jobs in what would become a tedious routine for some.

If you're looking for a simulation where you are a hacker paid by big companies to take on big jobs against individuals and other companies, look to Uplink for that, especially with the UplinkOS GUI mod.

And then this is where I tell you "but if you're looking for...", cause it's hard to pin Hacknet's strength. Like I said, it has good setups for its missions, but the actual main plot is honestly kind of weak. So why do I still recommend it? I guess it's in the charm of it all quite frankly between the music, the flashy aesthetic, and all that.

Like honestly, the ONLY reason I actually finally got through the main plot of this game was because a video got recommended to me of the games last mission out of context, and everything on screen along with Carpenter Brut's "Roller Mobster" was enough to make me think "What's going on?" and play though the game just to see what was up. And honestly it was a bit underwhelming once it was all said and done, lol

So do I still recommend this game?

It's 10USD, and it often goes on sale for like less than 2USD, so I'd either way.

Is the DLC worth it? I actually think the last mission of the DLC is better as it gives a far better "emotion" to you the player as you're doing it, so totally consider picking it up if it's on sale.

Also it's absolute bullcrap I can't do "rm -rf /" or any such variation of such. I don't care if teaching newbs the most dangerous command might make them also do it to their own terminal on accident, that's their fault and mine if I'm not paying attention.

Seriously, it would have made the last mission just more hilarious to just do that, crack open a can of coke, and just watch and wait for everything to delete.
