This is one of the best games I've ever played and I recommend it to anyone relatively familiar with computers, especially anyone who's dabbled in Linux, command lines, or coding. Even if the extent of your experience is just installing mods for games or messing around with file trees.

Here's the deal. It's obviously not real hacking. It will not teach you how to hack irl, which is probably a good thing. However, it does a good job at capturing the feeling of having years of experience hacking and being able to do it relatively effortlessly.

The interface is a moderate challenge to figure out, but it's very important that the learning curve is there. You actually need to learn a little bit of the command structures and how to run your hacking programs. Once you complete your first several hacks, most of the hacking itself becomes second nature. You know exactly how to break into basically anything. This is where the game really takes off in my opinion.

Sure you can break into anything, but are you being paranoid about leaving no trace behind? Can you do it fast enough to not get caught? Can you figure out exactly what you need to do once you've broken in? You can't just break into computers and expect that everything will turn out alright. Once you get deeper into the game, the risk of being caught or counter-hacked becomes exponentially bigger as your targets become more and more advanced. You will need to restore your own files somehow. You will need to have a few defenses in place for when you're inevitably attacked. And the game will not necessarily teach you how to do that. You'll have to think on your feet and be creative with solutions. Often there are multiple solutions that will work, and they potentially have different outcomes.

This game does not hold your hand and it is all the better for it. If you need help, you can find it, sure. But the game won't give you anything for free. Figuring out how to use the tools at your disposal is part of the learning process and it's far better for it. Within 2 hours you'll feel like an amateur script kitty hacker that's untouchable, but by the 3rd and 4th hour you'll be humbled by how vulnerable you really are.

Overall it's a really fun and unique experience that imo would be worth the full asking price. However, it goes on sale every few months for like $1.49. At that price it's an absolute steal and worth every penny. If you're even remotely interested in hacking and computers, pick it up sometime.

UPDATE - A couple of days after I post this review, the developer announces that he patched the bug that made the game impossible to complete. While another bug does exist at present (where if you do not accept the Junebug mission in time, you lose the opportunity to continue with the main story), it is possible to work around this by reloading an old save.

Upon reaching the end of the game, I am absolutely convinced that this game is one of (if not) the best hacking simulators on the market. The final mission in the game is so intense. I had to do it in several parts and my heart was racing each time I started it. There was nothing I could suggest to make the gameplay itself any better. Maybe adding in more missions to give it some replayability and a bit more freedom to go off and hack to your hearts content for good or for evil. However, that could be a DLC pack and can easily be added in. As the game stands, it deserves an 8/10, purely because it's still not perfect in terms of the bugs. However, they should be fixed soon given the dedication the dev has with this game.

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

Let me be perfectly clear with this before you read any further. I LOVE Hacknet. It's a fantastic game and is definitely better than Uplink by a mile. The use of real computer commands makes it feel much more realistic and the storyline is pretty awesome to boot. Plus, the time limit you have when a trace counter starts rapidly going down and you're waiting for the password crack to finish so you can intercept the trace creates one heck of an adrenaline rush.

However I cannot recommend it as it is now. There is a single bug I have encountered that makes the game impossible to complete. I will try to avoid giving away any spoilers, so this will be a bit vague. Later in game you are required to take on a mission that is part of the main storyline. However, you do not choose when this mission comes to you. It is automatically sent to you in an email and I'm not 100% sure what the criteria is for it appearing. To complete it, you need an .exe file used to crack a specific port which is only available by taking on a side mission. However, this mission is locked and once again, I do not know what the criteria is to unlock it. So I tried to take on the other available missions in an attempt to unlock the one I needed. In order to do this, you must abort the main storyline mission. Aborting a mission means you can NEVER attempt it again, making it impossible to continue with the main storyline. While I discovered it is possible to obtain the .exe without the mission, following an online walkthrough to obtain the information needed to get it instead of getting it in game feels wrong on so many levels, especially since it's deeply hidden within this seemingly permanently locked mission.

So at this time, I can't recommend it. The game is good, but I haven't been able to finish it because of this bug. The developer seems to be quite willing to take feedback and work on it so if you're reading this, I eagerly await a patch for this game. I can't wait to finish it.

review_text_raw:
I normally don't like puzzle games, because eventually a puzzle loses me once and then I never get back into the groove. Hacknet is possibly the first puzzle game that I have enjoyed since the days of Popcap. It helps that it is usually very easy, as long as you have experience with computers, and gives you specific instructions as to how to beat the levels beyond "hack everything you can". 
I have only two gripes. First is that the RAM management aspect (you only have a limited amount of ram, so you have to figure out the best parallel computing strategies when you're under a time limit) also cuts into your note-taking extensively. A single paragraph of notes takes up so much RAM that you can only use the smaller programs until you get it out of your face. The boss level fell flat as a pancake after I lost because I couldn't remember the name of a program that I needed and the list I had written for just such an occasion was deleted for taking up too much RAM. Why even have notes make such an impact on RAM economy if the player can just open up the notepad on his real desktop and use that?
Besides that bizarre choice, the network UI is appaling. In the screenshots, all those dots in the bottom of the screen are computers, there is no way to see what they are without mousing over them, you can't move them around, and they frequently overlap each other. That's another way the boss level fell flat: I just quit midway through because I had accidentally spent half the timer hacking the server that it had been placed on top of. You are just expected to remember where everything is, which wasn't easy when I had another game session the very next day, so I bet it's hellish if you have to wait a week to get back into it.
As for the good parts, it is very cool that you can play the entire game through console if you want to. Of particular note are the commands to open and close the CD tray. Apparently they actually work, even in multiplayer. There's even a branching storyline, as well as a substantial library of mods which are still being added to to this day. If you like the gameplay, then you can keep going until you don't anymore without having to retread the same ground more than a few times.

The boss level fell flat as a pancake after I lost because I couldn't remember the name of a program that I needed and the list I had written for just such an occasion was deleted for taking up too much RAM. Why even have notes make such an impact on RAM economy if the player can just open up the notepad on his real desktop and use that? Besides that bizarre choice, the network UI is appaling. In the screenshots, all those dots in the bottom of the screen are computers, there is no way to see what they are without mousing over them, you can't move them around, and they frequently overlap each other. That's another way the boss level fell flat: I just quit midway through because I had accidentally spent half the timer hacking the server that it had been placed on top of. You are just expected to remember where everything is, which wasn't easy when I had another game session the very next day, so I bet it's hellish if you have to wait a week to get back into it. As for the good parts, it is very cool that you can play the entire game through console if you want to. Of particular note are the commands to open and close the CD tray. Apparently they actually work, even in multiplayer. There's even a branching storyline, as well as a substantial library of mods which are still being added to to this day. If you like the gameplay, then you can keep going until you don't anymore without having to retread the same ground more than a few times.

Hacknet is an absolute gem of a game. 

[b]TLDR: [/b]While people already familiar with using *nix or general programing principles may find this game not too deep or challenging, it offers a well thought out narrative, with fun game mechanics and excels at teaching you about computer essentials without you even realizing it. 


[b]More thoughts:[/b] 

While this game isn't perfect, I would still reccomend it to anyone who has even a remote interest in computers. Even if you only want to feel like a hacker in a movie, that game gives you that feeling. If you want to learn more about the general concepts of computer-, program-, and network-architecture, this game is a great launching-point, before you start reading more "serious" or conventional literature on the subject. 

Now, the mechanics are pretty straight-forward. You gain various programs through completing quests, which, in turn, can be used to bypass more complex security. You also gain the ability to run commands through other computers, allowing you, for example, to pretty much emulate a DDOS attack. Timing is also important, so be ready to type "dc" + [enter] if you're being tracked. AAAAAAAAANNNNNNDDDDDD............

.....
.....
.....

that's pretty much it when it comes to mechanics. The rest is working your way through systems full of mostly text-files, a lot of them taken from bash.org (hilarious quotes from internet chats, NSFW, but great!), and a lot of fun easter-eggs for nerds and fans of "hacker-culture" as it has been created by Hollywood. There even are multiple references to the movie "Hackers", a must see in my opinion. ;)

Now, the mechanics got old after not too long (a good 8 hours), mainly due to you unlocking a lot of the tools that you need pretty quickly. I'll talk more about overall gameplay features in just a moment. 

The narrative is fun, well paced, and interwoven well with the gameplay mechanics. I won't spoil anything, just watch the trailer and you get the general premise. 

The overall game is simplified, to allow people without prior experience to enjoy it, but encourages experimentation and exploration of what you can do, giving you plenty of examples and hints along the way to teach you, without you even realizing it, a lot about how your system works. Absolutely amazing!

Concerning the lack of gameplay features, the dev is amazing. Yup, one dev. And he's already said that he wants to implement multiplayer. If that happens, this will become one of the best games out there. Period. Plus he wants to continue to push content for the game. Not to mention, that the community as a whole is awesome and really suportive for newcomers. 

In its current state, it's well worth the price its asking for. As the dev continues to push more content, the game will continue to expand and improve. 

Please support this game, as its honestly trying to be different and fun, without a lot of the backstabbing and abusive tactics emplyed by all too many triple AAA studios/publishers. I can guarantee, you'll have a blast playing this!

I would just like to point towards the roadmap the dev has for 2016, which includes multiplayer and steam-workshop integration for custom missions throughout various points this year. http://steamcommunity.com/games/365450/announcements/detail/955130645658936382

 WIll not actually refund any purchases if you are somehow not pleased with the overall game.

Batteries not included.

review_text_raw:
Where should I start.  My background is in hacking, and Hacknet annoyed me.  I already know unix commands, I felt entitled enough at the start to scoff at the simulated terminal's shortcomings.  No top? No df/du? No ability to create directories even? Pfft.

But then I stopped and listened.  I remembered the kick-ass tunes in the best hacking films of yesteryear, particularly Hackers, and I stopped expecting realism and just tried to enjoy the game for the atmosphere.  And there were moments during my first play through where I actually, uncontrollably, smiled like a kid at christmas.  You see, the beauty in this  game is that thinking like a hacker gets you places, and it's rewarding to once more feel that, even if just for a short time.  I won't spoil the game for anybody, but there were 3 points during my playthrough where I felt ridiculously happy.  The rest of it was entertaining but would have been bland if not for a compelling story and surprisingly good characterisation, given the short nature of the game.  But that's also my greatest criticism.  I can forgive the subset of 'nix commands, the hokey visualisations that accompany your hacking tools and the ultra cheesy faux corporation names, but the real problem it the game leaves you wanting a hell of a lot more when it's over.  There is a multiplayer version in the pipe (see what I did there), but I wasn't able to find much on upcoming features other than the dev is currently working on ports for mac and linux, which is fine but doesn't interest me since I mostly game on windoze.  But I want more plots, more things to hack, more tools.  I want modding, I want more of that amazing retro-themed music (particularly that ONE track, again, no spoilers. If you've completed the game, you know the one).  I want that track to kick in more than once a play-through, when I'm doing something crazy important and urgent in the game.  

TL;DR? Ex-hacker got nostalgic playing indie hacking game, had feels, loved it enough to write a review. 
5/10 for replayability of the game as it is currently.
10/10 for some obvious and not-so-obvious references to Hackers and other hacking esotera.

Overall, 10/10 if, and when, RPG-like elements like upgrading equipment, infinite procedural mission/story generation, and bouncing connections/more advanced tracing dynamics are introduced.  I know, I'm demanding.
For now? 8/10 for the most fun 6 hours of a game I've had since Portal 2.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a hacking simulation in the vein of Introversion's fantastic Uplink. It provides the player a virtual OS from which to interact with 'nodes' dotted around the map. Each node represents a computer system which can be approached using the software and hardware knowledge you accumulate throughout the game. Pretty simple stuff on the surface, but Hacknet is a fantastically well-designed story-driven experience, with considerable replay value which will only continue to grow as new content is invariably released.

This game deserves praise for it's graphics, in that they perfectly fit the tone of the game. In most other game genres we typically see a push toward more cutting-edge photo-realism, but here we have a clean, crisp environment that doesn't over-burden or confuse the player with menus and tedious repetitive interaction. Praise is also due to the sound design in this title. The music is, again, a perfect fit for the game's tone. Orchesteral strings move to thumping bass adding a sense of pressure and drive that has kept me going back just for the music.


There are some problems with this game however. Some people will say these aren't problems as such, more personal gripes, but take them however you wish. 

1. It's short. Like really short. With no experience whatsoever, my first run was just under 3 hours from start to finish, completing every avaliable mission in the game aside from 'Junebug' which was bugged at the time. Hopefully, more content will be added soon, and the ability to open story creation to the community is an exciting prospect shound it be considered.

2. It's easy. The learning curve is pretty shallow, with a few basic commands covering every action you will be performing. Once you have got launching cracks using the TAB key down to a fine art, you can smash through any security in next to no time.

3. No Upgrade abilities. A key component of every computer interface is the hardware it's connected to, and in a game setting the ability to upgrade and customise that hardware is a given. There is no such system here. The only resource you have is RAM, which is set throughout the game and cannot be improved upon. This does give the game a streamlined feel, but I would still rather have an functioning economy and avenues to explore with my earnings.

Overall, I think Hacknet deserves your time if you enjoy the genre. If you do enjoy this quite esoteric game style, then you've no doubt played the alternatives. On balance, I would say that Onlink, the fan-made re-write of Uplink is the superior game in this category still. It is a longer, more challenging experience. That being said, with expansion and dedication, Hacknet will become the standard by which all other hacking simulation games will be judged. We should all help it get there, and enjoy the rewards when they come.

Buy it.

Having sat through the entire game in one sitting, I can definitely reccomend playing the game to anyone who's into classic command line style games, althought it does require a tiny bit of technical knowhow, such as what directories are, what commands need in order to run (In a [Program Name] [Port Number/File Name] [Password] format), and memorising at least 8 or 9 commands you'll be using frequently throughout mid to end game. 

This would be fine if the commands were one word bt the majority of them consist of 1-3 words and may or may not have an underscore, making simple things like uploading files with long names a chore.

I think it's definitely doable if you've got some dexterity and typing speed, as you're required to do a lot in the space of 30 seconds. 

Pros:
- It's got a good story behind the scenes, and rewards you for going out of your way to find bits and pieces, looking in places you shouldn't, etc.
- The game itself doesn't take up a lot of space, and doesn't require a good computer to run.
- It teaches you a lot about the "society" around hacking, giving off a more "for the people" mindset that really makes you think about the ethics of hacking
- It has an inbuilt clicker game for free. (Which you can also hack like literally everything else)
- There's a dedicated wiki and fanbase around the game already, making searching for help that much more easier for new players.
- You're rewarded for playing the game a second time, with some extra content (though you may have already found it without the hint given to you), giving it some replayability rather than a "play it once and put it down" game.

Cons:
- It's repetitive, there's no getting around it for a text based game, however some long winded file names make it much worse, there is a shortcut where you press tab and it autocompletes, but 6 times out of 10 it just doesn't work.
- There isn't a lot of customisability until much later on in the game.
- There's a site in the game that literally rips off the 4chan format, although I admit the colour scheme is kinda cool.
- The tutorial doesn't tell you about commands that are pretty essential to the gameplay, I had to use guides to figure some bits out.

Overall, I'd give it a solid 8/10.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FxtyeJsem0U

[i]Hacknet[/i] is perhaps the first actual hacking game I've played outside of [i]Terminal Hacker[/i] (which was basically a guessing game similar to hangman).  It utilizes actual UNIX formatting in a mixture between a command prompt and a GUI layout.  In a way, it reminds me of my final heartbreaking days as an Information Technology major.

The story follows you, an unknown and obscure user who nobody would suspect of anything...until you get a message from a mysterious, yet well-known hacker who passed away.  Of all the people he chose as his spiritual successor, he chose you...someone who most likely has no connection to him whatsoever.  It's your job to avenge the fallen hacker's death and to honor his last wishes...while helping others or causing trouble along the way.

The hacking procedures are quite interesting and easy to learn, but become annoying after a while given that it's the same protocols every time with some new tricks thrown in every now and then.  Without a guide, [i]Hacknet[/i] really requires you to think and to look back at old references in your e-mails.   Soon enough, you'll encounter new obstacles, like increased security and even tracing, which adds a time limit and pressure to battle against.

Though I enjoyed [i]Hacknet[/i], I don't see too much replayability in it.  I was also not pleased with the repetitive nature of the game and there were cryptic moments where I needed to refer to a guide to proceed.  Cryptic and repetitive moments will quickly find themselves at your doorstep, but that's the name of the game, I suppose.

So...worth the price?  I suppose, but the repetitive bits make this [i]Hacknet[/i] rather unappealing.  It starts out simple, but you just end up doing the same thing for about 80% of the game...though the stressful tracing does make it a little more fun as some hacking tools require more time than others...so you have to balance your RAM as you try to hack through security.  Various bits aren't properly explained, too.  You sometimes need a new hacking method, but it's just not properly explained in my opinion.  It's moments like that that made me drop my IT major in college.  But to the point?  It's worth the price, but if you're a bargain hunter, $5 may be ideal.  Overall, I loved the idea and the execution was pretty good...but I wished that it was balanced a little more with even more to offer.

8/10  To be an expert hacker, you'll need a combination of the right software and wits...only one of them is provided by this game, the other must come from you.

A short but sweet game that may be especially interesting for people new to the command line / terminal interface. While the 'hacking' is somewhat shallow, the story is interesting. Intense time-pressure situations force you to apply your new knowledge, and fast; you must find, copy, delete, modify, scan, etc. before you're traced. It feels great to build up new hacking programs; Hacknet reveals its secrets at a natural pace.

The early missions are basic, to help you warm up your execution speed. When missions become complex (breadcrumb trails from one computer to the next), take unexpected turns, or introduce surprising new concepts and goals, Hacknet becomes truly excellent. It is not a stretch to say that the entire purpose of Hacknet is to prepare you for three or four outstanding missions - if the regular missions are engaging, these special ones inspire everything from terror to intense focus: they strain your hacking speed, your memory as you piece together a puzzle of scattered info, and inspire that conspiratorial feeling of getting closer to the hidden truth.

Hacknet doesn't outstay its welcome - it ends when all the available mechanics have been thoroughly explored and challenged, and no later. The campaign can be cleared in about six hours, and the remaining secrets and alternate paths can be tackled in another three hours (postgame knowledge and skills allow you to blast through the early missions in minutes, on subsequent playthroughs - this also feels great). 

Though its short length and limited replayability keep Hacknet out of 'classic territory', I would recommend it as a fun, fast way to get familiar with the basic concepts of terminal navigation and file editing(!). [Note: I was familiar with terminals before playing]

Hints for new players: 
1.) Don't forget about 'ps' and 'kill', they may save your life.

2.) If you find yourself in contact with a new faction or individual you want to follow-up with, do not complete or initiate missions with any other factions. [i]Completing one faction's mission while multiple paths are available will lock you into that faction's path[/i], closing off the others. [spoiler]You'll eventually end up in CSEC, no matter what[/spoiler]

3.) Use addNote for the tough stuff, but try to use your own memory whenever you can. It never hurts to download a file so you have a password on record.

4.) When in doubt, 'dc'.

review_text_raw:
I'll admit, I was not expecting much from a free humble game, especially one developed by a single person. Yet, I am plesantly suprised by the gameplay overall. This game is a hacking-puzzle game with a story essentially. 

When it comes to the hacking part, the mechanics feel cool to use and at times when hacking servers it can get intense and the learning curve as a result is well made. 

The puzzle part is also great, the game will tell you what you need to initally do in a mission and what the end goal is, but it heavily relies on your past experience with game mechanics and a bit of snooping on files to navigate through a misson.

The story itself is a 7.5 out of 10 but the story telling is 9 out of 10. To get the story in this game, you'll have to snoop on files like you would do in regular missons, with some files pointing in other directions for more bits of the story and since you are already conditioned to snoop around, the way the story is told fits the context well.

Replayability is quite good, passwords, usernames (non generic ones) and a bunch of information in missions is randomly generated which can be refreshing, but also the game has multiple paths with an obvious linear path and a secretive path which means you'll be going back to the game to find its secrets. 

It also has some humorous parts of the game which did may be giggle a bit.

I only have a couple issues:

- The saving system is a one slot system, so when I was at the point in the story where the secret path can be taken I couldn't make two game saves, and for the sake of the story line I went with the normal path on my first go.
- On some themes (the way the UI is arranged) tags on the map appear to be unreadable due to the names being cut off
- Achievement recognition is buggy, if you are a completionist, better prepare to pull your hair out

review_text_raw:
A hacker named Bit is dead. His computer had an automated script which sends a random person a set of instructions. YOU are the one selected to follow out his last will.

The game is a good hacking simulation, with a good command line system, a well-designed UI for those who aren't quite used to the command line yet, and a very well-designed web of connections. IP addresses, names, and quests are randomized each time so everyone's experience is slightly different. They even have some funny conversations in text files on some PCs. All the scripts you need to complete the game are easily accessible, whether you get them from hidden locations or you find them in organization databases. There are even some interesting things you can do with the command line and some interesting moments where it pays to have a bit of extra knowledge going in. And easter eggs. MANY easter eggs. Seriously, when you think you've found it all, something new catches your eye.

Through my playthroughs I did not check if there was a way to create automated scripts for some of these things. If it was possible, I completely missed it, and if it wasn't, it is something I would fault this game for at least slightly. However, it not being there does not detract from the rest of the game, as hacking tools are abundant. The story is really good, and all of the design moments know just how to kick your brain into overdrive.

Overall, I'd give it a 10/10. This is one of my favorite games to date. If you are willing to learn the command line, generally good practices, and pay close attention to everything you find, this game will be a blast. I HIGHLY recommend learning how to use the command line instead of relying on the UI, as there are some things that will definitely be much better if you do so. A second or third playthrough also still hits pretty good, as you can look back at when things were introduced, catch things you wouldn't have caught before, and overall experience it in a completely different way. After you've played the DLC and the game itself once or twice though, the replayability goes down heavily, but there is a TON of mods in the community if you want to see what others have made.

Go out there and leave no trace behind.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a cool little immersive puzzler that does a great job of making you feel like a Hollywood hacker. It can also help you learn a few basic CLI/terminal commands, and possibly improve your typing skills--especially if you don't use all of the shortcuts. ;)

The stylized interface is mostly intuitive and functional, although the flash sometimes gets in the way--especially while running programs. The map is a condensed and cluttered version of the one in Uplink, but usually performs its job well enough. Discovered themes/layouts can be swapped at will, but something with true customization would have been a better option. The music and sound effects fit the atmosphere, and there are even a few fairly memorable tunes.

Some functions are weirdly prohibitive--like even the smallest note can take up most of the tiny amount of RAM on your static system. Executing and killing processes from the command line is usually much faster than trying to click on the animated visual elements. Your hardware cannot be altered or upgraded, and while you can explore and find tons of little secrets and easter eggs--including stashes of interesting data files or progs--there is very little sense of actual progression beyond the linear story missions. The integrated Mod support could help, but I have yet to try any of them, so I can't comment on their value.

There are bugs, and it is possible to actually break your game while messing with your in-game system (so that's more like a feature.) IMPORTANT: A long-standing bug can and will "corrupt" your save file if you use Cloud Saves. Disable that junk, unless you like the added challenge of fixing your save file with a text editor. I figured it out on my own by comparing saves from the GOG version that I played a few years ago, but if that doesn't sound fun, then kill cloud support.

Overall--it's a fun niche title with mystery, intrigue, humor, and secrets that allows you to play out a few vanilla hacker fantasies. Definitely worth playing if you're an Uplink fan or looking for something different.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is an Immersive hacking simulation game that overall I felt could have done more. 

The idea of the game is cool and it does make you feel like a cool hacker, breaking into the mainframe with your tons of different tools and being able to say "I'm in" afterwards is always great and the game lets you feel that, so that much is admirable. But the game just gets repetitive, I started realizing that everything I was hacking into felt the same, you run the same programs and all you have to do to run them is type them in, you overload a proxy just by pressing a few buttons, and breaking a firewall was the closest thing to a "puzzle" in this process. I do like the variety in the sites you hack, from web browser games, to servers, to suspiscous websites. It certainly looked different, but it never felt that. The games interface I found simple and pretty easy to use, and considering that it is the whole game, it should be easy to use. The music was also pretty good but felt a little repetitive and generic after a while. The story is somewhat interesting but you've probably seen it before, and it is suuuuuper dragged out, as the whole point of the game starts at the beginning but disappears until the end, it's dragged out. Not to say that I didn't like the last few missions as those were actually a bit challenging. i just wish the game did more with its cool setting, ideas and possibly story. It has it's moments like when you first start hacking, getting attacked by Naix and the entire ending, but that's about it, also sometiems the solutions to things are WAYYY to specific and finnicky.

Pros
Good setting
Good ideas
Decent interface
Good music
Immersive

Cons
Gets repetitve
Story is way to underdeveloped and not paced well
Didn't do enough different thing's with what it had
A bit finnicky in solutions

Overall I'd give this a 6/10. I think it manages to be above average as it also serves as an entertaining enough time waster, I'd say buy it on a good sale and play it once, but probably not replay. However, this did convince me enough to look at other hacking games, like the DLC for this one, which I'll also review, so thank you for that!

Thanks For Reading!!
